claims.text: The central concept of write-ahead logging is that changes to data files must be written only after those changes have been logged, that is, after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage.

Data pages do not need to be flushed to disk on every transaction commit, because after a crash any changes not yet applied to the data pages can be redone from the log records. This is roll-forward recovery, also known as REDO.
It significantly reduces the number of disk writes, because only the log file needs to be flushed to guarantee that a transaction is committed, not every data file the transaction changed.
The log file is written sequentially, so syncing it costs much less than flushing the data pages, and one fsync of the log may suffice to commit many small concurrent transactions.
The log also makes online backup and point-in-time recovery possible.

answer.text: Changes to data files must be written only after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage.

recall.prompt: Why does a write-ahead log make commits cheaper, not more expensive?

answer.text: Only the log file must be flushed to commit, not every changed data file; the log is written sequentially; and one fsync may commit many concurrent transactions.

recall.prompt: After a crash, how are committed changes that never reached the data pages recovered?

answer.text: They are redone from the log records (roll-forward recovery, REDO).
